transcript:
Meeting header
Date: 2026-06-05 15:30 UTC
Duration: ~72 minutes
Attendees: Samira (Redwood AE), Diego (Redwood SE), Priya (Redwood), Karen (Atlas Head of Platform), Tom (SRE), Aisha (Security), James (ML)

Summary:
Quick deep dive on multi-region routing and failover options for Atlas Health; focus on policy routing, capacity considerations, KV cache behavior across regions, batching/latency tradeoffs, and an initial DR playbook for dedicated + private deployment. Action items and pilot next steps captured.

Topics (auto):
- Policy routing (latency vs cost)
- Regional capacity & burst models
- KV cache replication / warming strategies
- Batching and latency SLOs impact across regions
- Quantization and model variants for failover
- VPC/on-prem networking and DR playbooks

Transcript:
[00:00] Samira: hey everyone thanks for joining, uh we'll keep this tight, Diego's gonna walk through our recommended multi-region setup and then we can drill into KV cache stuff and DR runs.
[00:34] Diego: cool, hi i'm diego from redwood infra, um quick note, apologies small audio glitch at the start for me. so high level we think of routing as policy first — latency policy, cost policy, and compliance policy. latency policy says route to lowest RTT region, cost policy can prefer cheaper spot capacity or quantized model variants. compliance policy pins to region or private deployment.
[01:12] Karen: can you define "quantized variant" again? we talked about this with James but want the refresher for the execs.
[01:20] Diego: sure, quantized variant is a model built w/ lower precision (eg 8-bit or 4-bit int) that lowers gpu memory and increases throughput, often with slight quality delta. for failover we use a chain: primary full precision -> quantized compatible variant -> smaller model family as last resort. that way we can keep latency SLOs while protecting availability.
[02:05] Tom: are you folks doing automatic fallback between those? like if primary region overloaded, route to quantized in same region or go cross region?
[02:15] Samira: good question. policy-driven. default is same-region fallback to a compatible variant to keep data residency. if same-region capacity exhausted we failover cross-region to a pinned allowed region, following compliance rules.
[02:40] Aisha: what's the impact on KV cache when you do cross-region failover? our session affinity relies on cached KV for context.
[02:50] Diego: yeah that's the tricky part. KV cache is per-serving runtime instance; we don't replicate live KV across regions by default because of performance and consistency. our suggested patterns: 1) sticky sessions so that short-lived sessions remain in-region and cache hits stay high; 2) proactive cache warming for known hot prefixes when failing over; 3) cold-start mitigation by running async cache prefetch jobs after failover; 4) fall back to shorter context window if cache miss rates spike.
[03:45] James: when you say "proactive warming" how do you populate the KV in remote region quickly?
[03:53] Diego: two ways: push recent hot prefixes via our background replication pipeline (eventually-consistent) or replay recent traffic via an ingest replayer into the remote runtime's cache. both require careful PII handling — we scrub or tokenise depending on your compliance needs.
[04:30] Karen: scrub how? PII is big for us. Aisha will need to sign off.
[04:36] Aisha: yep, we need KMS/HSM integration and audit logs for any cache replication. also retention windows. is that supported?
[04:45] Priya: short answer yes — in Private deployments we can integrate with customer KMS, and replication tooling can be configured to avoid storing raw PII. we also emit audit trails for those jobs.
[05:05] Tom: what about latency impact of sticky sessions? our traffic is 60% US-EAST, 30% EU-WEST, 10% APAC. sessions average 22s with lots of streaming.
[05:20] Diego: sticky sessions reduce cross-region churn but can cause imbalance; we recommend a hybrid policy: session-affinity for first N minutes (say 5-10m) then global balancing for longer-lived background inference. also autoscale pools per region with reserve burst capacity so short surges stay local.
[05:55] Karen: curious on the math — how much reserve do you typically recommend?
[06:03] Diego: depends on your p95 QPS and tail latency SLO. typical approach: reserve capacity for 20-30% of p95 p90 traffic and allow burst to shared pool with cost controls. we'll share a sample calc sheet.
[06:25] Samira: note we'll also factor in continuous batching behavior — batching increases throughput but can raise 95th pct latency, so tradeoffs matter when routing across regions.
[06:40] James: can you show an example where batching hurt failover latency?
[06:45] Diego: yes — imagine a remote region with low traffic that only forms large batches every few hundred ms; if you suddenly route lots of single-user low-latency requests there, they'll wait to form batch and you see a latency bump. mitigation: adaptive batch timers and small-slab immediate path for <X tokens or high-priority routes.
[07:10] Tom: talk to me about network egress & cross-region costs; we have tight budgets.
[07:17] Samira: cost is why we prefer same-region variant fallback first. cross-region routing triggers egress and inter-region replication costs. policy can prefer cheaper variants or degrade to streaming with lower tokenization to save egress. also you can set SLO-based constraints in the route rules.
[07:45] Karen: ok, what does the DR playbook look like? step me through an outage scenario where us-east is down.
[07:53] Diego: simple playbook: 1) detect via health-check + traffic anomalies; 2) initial automated fallback: route to in-region quantized variants (if any) or in-region reserved spare capacity; 3) if region is unhealthy, activate cross-region failover to pre-authorized regions (we keep allowlist); 4) run cache warming job and session replay for critical prefixes; 5) escalate to on-call and run post-mortem. we'll provide a templated runbook with run commands.
[08:40] Aisha: who triggers the cross-region failover — automatic or manual? we need SSO approval in some scenarios.
[08:46] Diego: it's configurable. for P0s we recommend automatic failover if latency > X and error rate > Y for Z minutes; for compliance-restricted routes we do manual failover requiring approval (e.g., SRE + Security).
[09:10] Karen: how long until things are stable after failover — our compliance teams will ask about RTO/RPO.
[09:16] Diego: RTO often 30-90s for traffic reroute; full warming and cache parity can take minutes depending on state. RPO depends on whether you replicate or replay events — typically eventual, so some in-flight context could be lost. we document expected degradation modes.
[09:45] James: can we keep user-visible sessions intact?
[09:49] Diego: best effort. sticky sessions + routing tokenization help. for strong guarantees you'd need global KV replication, which is doable but expensive and increases consistency complexity. we tend to recommend selective replication for a small set of keys (top N hot users) rather than full state.
[10:20] Tom: what about private/on-prem deployments — how do they fit into routing & failover?
[10:26] Priya: if you're on-prem in a region, the control plane can run in our hosted control plane while runtimes are customer-managed. routing policies can pin sensitive workloads to private clusters; during DR you can either failover to another private cluster or to dedicated hosted capacity depending on policy and agreements. network peering and VPN degradations are the common failure modes we plan for.
[11:00] Aisha: and audit/compliance for that mixed mode?
[11:03] Priya: we capture change logs, who initiated failovers, and KMS key usage. we'll hand over an audit package for your SOC reviews.
[11:20] Karen: any gotchas on quantization models across regions? like different perf on different GPUs?
[11:28] Diego: yeah different hardware and kernel selection affects perf; our runtime compiles kernels per target, so we surface model variant perf profiles by region. during routing we consult the perf profile and estimated latency; if a quantized variant on region B is slower than full precision in region C, policy may prefer C despite higher egress. it's policy-weighted.
[12:05] Tom: curious about observability — can we see token-level latency per region in console?
[12:09] Samira: yes console shows per-route, per-model token latency, tail percentiles, and cost breakdown. plus tracing hooks for request-level diagnostics. we'll share screenshots.
[12:22] Karen: any security items to note for cross-region replication?
[12:26] Aisha: I specifically want to avoid any inadvertent exposure of PHI. is the replication encrypted end-to-end?
[12:32] Priya: yes, TLS in flight and KMS-managed envelopes at rest. for PHI we recommend private network replication and limited key unwrap privileges.
[12:45] Diego: also keep in mind tokenization and scrub steps before warming caches. we can optionally hash keys so that raw PII never leaves primary region.
[13:05] James: from an ML perspective, do you version the cache schema? what if model rollout changes prefix shapes?
[13:11] Diego: we version cache schema and KV keys; our runtime supports migration paths and graceful invalidation. model rollouts include cache compatibility checks as part of canary.
[13:35] Tom: one more thing — how does batching across regions work if you enable cross-region routing?
[13:41] Diego: we avoid cross-region batching because network round-trips kill latency and throughput. batching happens per runtime pool. cross-region routing should prefer local batching and avoid pulling traffic back and forth.
[14:00] Karen: ok this is helpful. can you give a recommended starter config for Atlas Health given our traffic mix?
[14:05] Samira: recommended starter: reserve dedicated pools in US-EAST and EU-WEST with 25% reserved spare capacity, enable sticky sessions 10m for interactive flows, set automatic in-region fallback to quantized variants, allow cross-region failover to eu-west for compliance-exempt flows and to us-west as cost fallback, enable cache warming on failover for top 200 prefixes, and run pilot for 2 weeks.
[14:40] Diego: we'll attach perf numbers — expected p95 changes during failover and warmup. note: you can tune batch timers and priority lanes for latency-sensitive routes.
[15:00] Aisha: for the pilot we need the security package and object-level audit.
[15:04] Priya: yes we'll send the security package and a sample runbook for SOC review.
[15:12] Samira: ok let's wrap — recap next steps and owners.
[15:18] Karen: thanks, and Diego, Priya great detail.
